basic_information.name: RAG Taxonomy (Naive / Advanced / Modular)
basic_information.creator: Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Meng Wang, Haofen Wang et al. (Tongji University / Fudan University). The three-tier taxonomy was formalized in two key papers: the RAG survey (arXiv:2312.10997, December 2023) and the Modular RAG paper (arXiv:2407.21059, July 2024). The original RAG concept was introduced by Patrick Lewis et al. at Facebook AI Research (arXiv:2005.11401, May 2020).
basic_information.description: The RAG Taxonomy is a classification framework that organizes Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems into three evolutionary paradigms: Naive RAG (simple retrieve-then-generate pipeline), Advanced RAG (optimized pre-retrieval, retrieval, and post-retrieval stages), and Modular RAG (LEGO-like reconfigurable architecture with independent modules and operators). This taxonomy, formalized by Gao et al. in their widely-cited survey, provides the standard vocabulary for understanding how RAG systems have evolved from basic vector-similarity retrieval to sophisticated, composable architectures integrating routing, fusion, memory, and task adaptation. Naive and Advanced RAG are special cases of the more general Modular RAG framework. The taxonomy matters because it gives entrepreneurs and engineers a structured way to assess which level of RAG complexity their use case requires, avoiding both under-engineering (Naive RAG with poor accuracy) and over-engineering (Modular RAG when a simpler approach suffices).
basic_information.release_date: Original RAG concept: May 2020 (Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020). Three-tier taxonomy formalized: December 2023 (Gao et al. survey, arXiv:2312.10997). Modular RAG framework detailed: July 2024 (Gao et al., arXiv:2407.21059). Multiple revisions through 2024-2025.
basic_information.license: Not applicable (conceptual classification framework). The survey papers are freely available on arXiv under standard academic open access. Implementations of each paradigm are available across open-source frameworks (LangChain MIT, LlamaIndex MIT, Haystack Apache 2.0, etc.).
basic_information.github_stars: Not applicable directly (conceptual framework). The NirDiamant/RAG_Techniques repository documenting many of these patterns has ~10,000+ stars. Frameworks implementing these patterns: LangChain ~118k, LlamaIndex ~40k, Haystack ~20k (as of early 2026).

technical_architecture.architecture_type: Conceptual classification framework spanning three paradigms. (1) Naive RAG: linear pipeline (Index -> Retrieve -> Generate), tightly coupled, sequential execution. (2) Advanced RAG: enhanced linear pipeline with pre-retrieval optimization (query rewriting, expansion), retrieval optimization (hybrid search, fine-tuned embeddings), and post-retrieval optimization (reranking, compression). (3) Modular RAG: decomposed into independent modules and specialized operators in a three-tier design (modules -> sub-modules -> operators), supporting non-linear flows with routing, scheduling, fusion, and feedback loops. The Modular RAG paper (arXiv:2407.21059) describes six core module types: Indexing, Pre-Retrieval, Retrieval, Post-Retrieval, Generation, and Orchestration, each with multiple sub-modules and operators.
technical_architecture.language: Language-agnostic conceptual framework. Implementations exist in Python (dominant: LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, DSPy), JavaScript/TypeScript (LangChain.js, Vercel AI SDK), Java (Spring AI), Rust (various vector store backends), Go (Weaviate, Milvus backends), and C++ (FAISS, vector indexing).
technical_architecture.embedding_dimensions: Not applicable directly (framework-agnostic). Naive RAG typically uses a single embedding model (768-1536 dimensions). Advanced RAG may use multiple embedding models or fine-tuned embeddings. Modular RAG supports multi-vector representations (ColBERT: 128 per-token, multi-representation indexing). Common dimensions across paradigms: 384 (MiniLM), 768 (BERT-base, BGE-base), 1024 (BGE-large, Jina v3), 1536 (OpenAI ada-002), 3072 (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large).
technical_architecture.indexing_algorithm: Varies by paradigm. Naive RAG: flat or simple HNSW index with single vector per chunk. Advanced RAG: HNSW with optimized parameters, hierarchical indexing (RAPTOR-style tree summaries), multi-index structures (parent-child document indexing), metadata-enriched indices. Modular RAG: supports any combination — HNSW, IVF-PQ, DiskANN, product quantization, binary quantization, graph-based indices (for GraphRAG), and hybrid indices combining dense vectors with sparse inverted indices (BM25/SPLADE).
technical_architecture.scalability: Naive RAG: limited scalability, single retrieval path, no sharding strategy. Advanced RAG: moderate scalability through optimized indexing and retrieval but still follows a fixed pipeline. Modular RAG: high scalability by design — independent modules can be scaled independently, supports distributed retrieval across multiple indices, parallel module execution, and dynamic routing to handle varying query loads. Enterprise deployments handle 10M-1B+ documents with Modular RAG patterns.
technical_architecture.deployment_options: All paradigms can be deployed anywhere Python/JS runs: local development, Docker, Kubernetes, serverless (AWS Lambda, GCP Cloud Functions), cloud-managed (LangGraph Cloud, LlamaCloud, Azure AI Search), edge (with small models). Naive RAG: simplest deployment, single service. Advanced RAG: typically 2-3 services (embedding, retrieval, generation). Modular RAG: microservices or monolith with modular internal structure, often requires orchestration layer (LangGraph, Haystack pipelines, or custom).

rag_specific_capabilities.retrieval_method: Naive RAG: dense vector similarity search only (cosine or dot product over pre-computed embeddings). Top-k retrieval with no reranking. Advanced RAG: hybrid retrieval combining dense vectors with sparse methods (BM25, SPLADE), query expansion (HyDE — Hypothetical Document Embeddings), multi-query retrieval (RAG-Fusion with reciprocal rank fusion), self-query (metadata filtering via natural language). Modular RAG: all Advanced RAG methods plus knowledge graph retrieval (GraphRAG, entity-based traversal), multi-hop reasoning chains (iterative retrieval), adaptive retrieval (deciding whether to retrieve at all), cross-encoder reranking as a dedicated module, and pluggable retrieval operators that can be swapped or combined via configuration.
rag_specific_capabilities.chunking_strategy_support: Naive RAG: fixed-size chunking (e.g., 512 tokens with overlap), typically character-based splitting. Advanced RAG: semantic chunking (embedding-based boundary detection), recursive character splitting respecting document structure, document-structure-aware splitting (Markdown headers, HTML sections, LaTeX), late chunking (embedding full documents then splitting), RAPTOR hierarchical summarization trees. Modular RAG: all of the above plus agentic chunking (LLM-decided boundaries), proposition-based chunking (decomposing text into atomic propositions), and custom chunking operators that can be plugged into the indexing module.
rag_specific_capabilities.reranking_support: Naive RAG: none (raw retrieval scores used directly). Advanced RAG: cross-encoder reranking (e.g., ms-marco-MiniLM), ColBERT-based reranking, LLM-as-judge reranking, reciprocal rank fusion for multi-query results, Cohere Rerank API, score fusion (combining dense and sparse scores). Modular RAG: dedicated reranking sub-module within Post-Retrieval module, supports chaining multiple rerankers, adaptive reranking depth, and integration with specialized models (Jina Reranker v3, BGE Reranker, RankGPT).
rag_specific_capabilities.multimodal_support: Naive RAG: text-only in the original formulation. Advanced RAG: supports multimodal retrieval via vision-language models (CLIP embeddings for images, table extraction via Unstructured/Docling), multi-modal document parsing. Modular RAG: native multimodal support through dedicated multimodal indexing and retrieval modules, support for image, table, chart, audio, and video embeddings. MMA-RAG (Multimodal Agentic RAG, 2025 survey) extends Modular RAG with specialized multimodal agents.
rag_specific_capabilities.graph_rag_support: Naive RAG: none. Advanced RAG: limited integration with knowledge graphs as an additional retrieval source. Modular RAG: full GraphRAG support as a pluggable module — includes entity extraction (via LLMs or NER models), relationship mapping, community detection (Leiden algorithm), hierarchical graph summarization, and graph-enhanced retrieval combining vector similarity with graph traversal. Microsoft's GraphRAG (2024) is the most prominent implementation, converting unstructured text into knowledge graphs with community summaries for global reasoning over large corpora.
rag_specific_capabilities.citation_grounding: Naive RAG: minimal — can show source documents but no structured citation. Advanced RAG: improved source attribution through chunk-level tracing, relevance scoring per source. Modular RAG: dedicated citation/grounding modules possible — SEER (Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for RAG) for faithful evidence extraction, chain-of-thought grounding where each claim links to specific retrieved passages, and integration with evaluation frameworks (RAGAS faithfulness metric). Grounding verification can be implemented as a post-generation validation module.
rag_specific_capabilities.context_window_optimization: Naive RAG: simple top-k concatenation, often exceeds context window or wastes tokens on irrelevant content. Advanced RAG: contextual compression (extracting relevant portions from retrieved chunks), map-reduce over long documents, iterative refinement chains, conversation summary memory. Modular RAG: dynamic context assembly via orchestration module — adaptive retrieval depth (retrieve more or fewer chunks based on query complexity), context compression operators, recursive summarization, lost-in-the-middle mitigation (reordering chunks to place most relevant at start and end), and predict modules that generate partial context to reduce retrieval dependence.

performance_and_benchmarks.latency: Paradigm-level latency characteristics: Naive RAG: fastest per-query (single retrieval + single generation pass), typical end-to-end 0.5-2 seconds depending on LLM. Advanced RAG: 1.5-5 seconds due to additional query transformation, hybrid retrieval, and reranking steps. Modular RAG: highly variable (1-15+ seconds) depending on module configuration — simple routing adds minimal overhead, while multi-hop retrieval with reranking and validation can take 10+ seconds. Agentic RAG (a Modular RAG pattern) can take 15-60+ seconds for complex multi-step reasoning. The key trade-off: Naive RAG optimizes for speed, Advanced/Modular RAG optimize for quality at the cost of latency.
performance_and_benchmarks.throughput: Naive RAG: highest throughput (simple pipeline, easily parallelizable), can handle hundreds of queries/second with cached embeddings and fast vector stores. Advanced RAG: moderate throughput reduction (2-3x more compute per query due to reranking and query expansion). Modular RAG: throughput depends on pipeline complexity — simple configurations match Advanced RAG, complex agentic configurations may require significant compute. Batch processing and asynchronous module execution can recover throughput in Modular RAG.
performance_and_benchmarks.accuracy_metrics: Naive RAG: reported answer accuracy as low as ~25% in enterprise deployments (per DevStark analysis), with significant hallucination risk due to noisy retrieval. Advanced RAG: 40-65% accuracy improvement over Naive RAG through reranking and query optimization (per LangChain compression studies showing 92-96% accuracy retention with significant token reduction). Modular RAG: highest potential accuracy through iterative refinement, but quality depends heavily on module selection and orchestration. Standard evaluation via RAGAS metrics: Faithfulness (factual consistency with retrieved context, 0-1), Answer Relevancy (response relevance to query, 0-1), Context Precision (fraction of relevant items in retrieved context), Context Recall (fraction of ground truth covered by retrieval). [uncertain]
performance_and_benchmarks.benchmark_results: No single benchmark directly compares all three paradigms in a controlled study. Relevant benchmarks: CRUD-RAG (tests Create/Read/Update/Delete scenarios), RAGBench with TRACe (12 domains, 100k examples), MIRAGE (medical RAG, 2024), Long2RAG (long-context RAG), BEIR (zero-shot retrieval across 18 datasets). The Gao et al. survey (2312.10997) provides qualitative comparison showing Modular RAG > Advanced RAG > Naive RAG on flexibility, accuracy, and adaptability, but the gap narrows for simple factoid QA where Naive RAG can be sufficient. DomainRAG (2024) benchmark specifically tests domain-specific challenges like time-sensitive queries and multi-document reasoning. [uncertain]

integration_and_ecosystem.framework_compatibility: All three paradigms are implementable in major frameworks: LangChain (LCEL chains for all levels, LangGraph for Modular/Agentic patterns), LlamaIndex (query pipelines and agent-based RAG), Haystack (component-based pipelines natural fit for Modular RAG), DSPy (programmatic prompt optimization applicable to all levels). Naive RAG: basic chain in any framework (~10 lines of code). Advanced RAG: requires framework-specific retriever wrappers, reranker integration. Modular RAG: best supported by LangGraph (graph-based orchestration with cycles), Haystack (pipeline DAGs), and DSPy (modular program composition).
integration_and_ecosystem.model_compatibility: All paradigms are model-agnostic. Naive RAG works with any LLM (even small 7B models) and any embedding model. Advanced RAG benefits from stronger LLMs for query rewriting (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2) and specialized embedding/reranking models (Cohere Embed v3, Jina v3, BGE-M3). Modular RAG can orchestrate multiple models for different modules — e.g., fast small model for routing, strong model for generation, specialized model for reranking. Compatible with all providers: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Meta (Llama), DeepSeek, open-source via Ollama/vLLM.
integration_and_ecosystem.mcp_integration_status: The RAG taxonomy itself is a conceptual framework, not a tool with MCP integration. However, frameworks implementing these paradigms are increasingly MCP-compatible: LangChain has langchain-mcp-adapters (March 2025), and Modular RAG patterns naturally align with MCP's tool-use paradigm where retrieval modules can be exposed as MCP tools for agent integration.
integration_and_ecosystem.data_source_connectors: Not applicable directly (conceptual framework). All paradigms rely on the underlying framework's data connectors. Naive RAG typically uses a single data source and vector store. Advanced RAG may integrate multiple data sources with metadata enrichment. Modular RAG supports dynamic data source routing — the routing module can direct queries to different indices, databases, APIs, or knowledge graphs based on query type. Common connectors across paradigms: S3, GCS, Confluence, Notion, Slack, web crawlers, SQL databases, and specialized document parsers.
integration_and_ecosystem.observability_integration: Observability needs increase with paradigm complexity. Naive RAG: basic logging of retrieval scores and generation output. Advanced RAG: trace each stage (query transformation, retrieval, reranking, generation) with tools like LangSmith, Langfuse, or Arize Phoenix. Modular RAG: requires full distributed tracing across modules — OpenTelemetry support, per-module latency tracking, module-level quality metrics, and debugging of routing decisions. LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, and Langfuse all support the trace granularity needed for Modular RAG debugging.

pricing_and_cost.pricing_model: The taxonomy itself is free (academic conceptual framework). Implementation costs vary dramatically by paradigm: Naive RAG has lowest infrastructure cost (single embedding model + vector store + LLM). Advanced RAG adds cost for reranking models, query expansion (additional LLM calls), and more complex infrastructure. Modular RAG has highest cost due to multiple specialized models, orchestration overhead, and potentially multiple retrieval passes. Cost structure: per-token (LLM calls), per-query (embedding + retrieval), per-GB (vector storage), per-compute-hour (hosting).
pricing_and_cost.free_tier: Naive RAG can be built entirely with free tiers: Chroma (local vector store), open-source embedding model (sentence-transformers), and a free LLM API tier or local model (Ollama + Llama 3). Advanced and Modular RAG can also start on free tiers but typically require paid services for production-quality reranking and orchestration.
pricing_and_cost.cost_at_scale: Naive RAG at 1M documents: vector store $50-200/month + embedding generation (one-time $10-50) + LLM calls $100-500/month = $150-750/month. Advanced RAG at 1M documents: add reranking costs ($50-200/month for API-based rerankers like Cohere or Jina), query expansion LLM calls (+30-50% on LLM costs), and more complex hosting = $300-1,500/month. Modular RAG at 1M documents: add orchestration compute, multiple model endpoints, potential GraphRAG infrastructure, iterative retrieval overhead = $500-5,000+/month depending on pipeline complexity. At 100M documents, costs scale roughly 10-50x depending on query volume and caching strategy.
pricing_and_cost.total_cost_of_ownership: Total RAG TCO includes: (1) Infrastructure: vector store, compute, networking. (2) Model costs: embedding generation, LLM inference, reranking. (3) Engineering time (largest component): Naive RAG 1-2 engineer-weeks to build, Advanced RAG 4-8 engineer-weeks, Modular RAG 8-16+ engineer-weeks. (4) Maintenance: data pipeline updates, model upgrades, evaluation cycles. (5) Evaluation infrastructure: RAGAS or custom evaluation, test datasets, annotation. For a typical startup: Naive RAG TCO ~$500-2,000/month all-in (including partial engineer time), Advanced RAG ~$2,000-8,000/month, Modular RAG ~$5,000-20,000+/month. Enterprise Modular RAG deployments often exceed $50,000/month including engineering overhead.

adoption_and_market.market_position: The Naive/Advanced/Modular taxonomy is the dominant classification framework in the RAG ecosystem, cited by virtually every major technical blog, framework documentation, and industry report. The Gao et al. survey (arXiv:2312.10997) is one of the most-cited RAG papers. The RAG market overall is estimated at $1.85-2.33 billion in 2025, growing at 35-50% CAGR to $9.86-67.42 billion by 2030-2034 (varying by analyst). As of 2025-2026, industry adoption is roughly: 40-50% Naive RAG (POCs and simple chatbots), 35-40% Advanced RAG (production enterprise systems), 10-20% Modular/Agentic RAG (cutting-edge deployments). The trend is clearly moving toward Advanced and Modular RAG as organizations graduate from POC to production. [uncertain]
adoption_and_market.notable_customers: Taxonomy is used universally as a conceptual reference. Notable adopters of each paradigm: Naive RAG: most chatbot MVPs, small startup internal tools, quick customer support bots. Advanced RAG: Klarna (customer support), Cisco (documentation search via LangChain), JPMorgan (financial document analysis), Harvey (legal AI). Modular/Agentic RAG: Microsoft (GraphRAG for scientific research via Discovery platform), Bloomberg (financial analysis with multi-source retrieval), large consulting firms (BCG, McKinsey for knowledge management).
adoption_and_market.community_size: The RAG research community is one of the largest in applied AI. Key indicators: the Gao et al. survey has 1,300+ citations on Semantic Scholar (as of early 2026). NirDiamant/RAG_Techniques GitHub repo: ~10k stars documenting advanced patterns. Active communities discussing RAG paradigms on Reddit (r/MachineLearning, r/LocalLLaMA), Hacker News, Discord servers of LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack. Multiple dedicated conferences and workshops (e.g., LangChain Interrupt, ACL RAG workshops). [uncertain]
adoption_and_market.funding_and_valuation: Not applicable directly (academic taxonomy). The broader RAG ecosystem has attracted massive funding: LangChain ($260M, $1.25B valuation), Pinecone ($138M, $750M valuation), Weaviate ($120M, Series C), Qdrant ($45M), Chroma ($18M), Vectara ($28.5M), Zilliz/Milvus ($113M). Total RAG ecosystem funding exceeds $1 billion. The taxonomy influences investment thesis: VCs increasingly evaluate startups based on which RAG paradigm they implement and whether their architecture supports progression from Naive to Modular.
adoption_and_market.competitive_landscape: Alternative RAG classification frameworks exist but are less widely adopted: (1) The REALM/FiD/RETRO lineage (model-integrated retrieval), (2) ACL KDD taxonomy (Retrieval-Augmented LLMs survey, Fan et al.), (3) Agentic RAG taxonomy (Singh et al., arXiv:2501.09136, January 2025) which extends Modular RAG into single-agent, multi-agent, and hierarchical agentic patterns, (4) Context Engineering paradigm (2025) which some argue supersedes RAG terminology. The Gao et al. Naive/Advanced/Modular taxonomy remains dominant because of its simplicity, clear evolutionary narrative, and broad adoption in industry discourse.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: The taxonomy is essential for startup decision-making. Recommendations by stage: (1) Pre-seed / MVP stage (0-3 months, 1-2 engineers, <$5k/month budget): Start with Naive RAG. Use LangChain or LlamaIndex basic RAG chain + a managed vector store (Pinecone free tier or Chroma local). Focus on validating that RAG solves the user problem before optimizing retrieval quality. This gets you from idea to testable product in 1-3 days. (2) Seed stage / product-market fit (3-12 months, 2-5 engineers, $5-20k/month budget): Graduate to Advanced RAG. Add hybrid search (BM25 + dense vectors), reranking (Cohere or cross-encoder), and semantic chunking. This addresses the most common Naive RAG failure mode (retrieving irrelevant chunks). (3) Series A+ / scaling (12+ months, 5+ engineers, $20k+/month budget): Consider Modular RAG only if your use case genuinely requires it — multi-domain queries, multi-hop reasoning, or agentic workflows. Most startups never need to leave Advanced RAG. Over-engineering to Modular RAG prematurely is a common and expensive mistake.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy_guidance: For Naive RAG: always build (it takes hours with existing frameworks, buying adds unnecessary vendor lock-in). For Advanced RAG: build the pipeline using open-source frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack) but buy infrastructure (managed vector stores like Pinecone or Weaviate Cloud, managed reranking APIs like Cohere). For Modular RAG: strongly consider buying a managed platform (Vectara, Azure AI Search, AWS Bedrock Knowledge Bases) unless you have dedicated ML engineering resources, as the orchestration complexity is substantial. Key decision factors: data sensitivity (self-host if HIPAA/GDPR critical), customization needs (build if domain-specific modules needed), time-to-market (buy for fastest launch, build for long-term flexibility). The most common failure mode is building a custom Modular RAG system when a managed Advanced RAG service would suffice.
entrepreneurial_relevance.time_to_production: Naive RAG: POC in 1-3 days, production-ready in 1-2 weeks. Advanced RAG: POC in 1-2 weeks, production-ready in 4-8 weeks (dominated by evaluation and tuning chunking/retrieval/reranking). Modular RAG: POC in 2-4 weeks, production-ready in 2-6 months (dominated by module integration, testing routing logic, and handling edge cases). Enterprise Modular RAG with compliance: 6-12 months. Critical insight from B Capital's startup survey: most RAG systems require 3-6 months of iterative refinement after initial deployment to reach acceptable quality, regardless of paradigm. The typical failure pattern is deploying Naive RAG, getting poor results, then scrambling to retrofit Advanced RAG techniques — it is better to plan for Advanced RAG from the start.
key_lessons: Match paradigm complexity to your actual needs. 80% of RAG use cases (internal document search, FAQ bots, customer support) are well-served by Advanced RAG. Only reach for Modular RAG when you have evidence that simpler approaches fail — multi-domain routing, multi-hop reasoning over 10+ document sources, or agentic workflows requiring tool use. Premature complexity is the top RAG startup killer.

The biggest ROI in RAG comes from investing in data quality, not architecture sophistication. Before upgrading from Naive to Advanced RAG, ensure your documents are properly cleaned, chunked with appropriate overlap, and enriched with metadata. A well-chunked Naive RAG system often outperforms a poorly-chunked Advanced RAG system.

Evaluation must drive paradigm evolution. Set up RAGAS metrics (Faithfulness, Answer Relevancy, Context Recall) from day one. Upgrade from Naive to Advanced RAG only when metrics show specific failure modes (low context precision -> add reranking, low recall -> add query expansion). Without metrics, you are optimizing blindly.

Plan your RAG migration path upfront. Use frameworks that support progressive complexity: start with a basic LangChain chain (Naive), add retriever wrappers and rerankers (Advanced), then migrate to LangGraph for orchestration (Modular). Switching frameworks mid-stream is extremely costly. Lock your core abstractions early.

Security scales with paradigm complexity. Naive RAG has a small attack surface (poisoned documents, basic prompt injection). Advanced RAG adds reranker manipulation vectors. Modular RAG with multiple data sources and agentic modules has the largest attack surface — each module is a potential injection point. Budget for security review proportional to your RAG paradigm complexity.
entrepreneurial_relevance.no_code_interface: The taxonomy itself has no interface (it is a conceptual framework). No-code RAG builders typically implement Naive or Advanced RAG: Langflow (visual LangChain builder), Flowise (drag-and-drop), Dify (open-source LLMOps with RAG), Vectara (managed platform with web UI), Azure AI Search (portal-based RAG setup). Full Modular RAG with custom routing and fusion generally requires code. LlamaCreate and similar emerging tools are attempting to make Advanced RAG patterns accessible via UI.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 1 (Fundamentals & AI Landscape): introduce the three paradigms as part of the AI ecosystem overview. Session 2 (Prompt Engineering & No-Code Tools): hands-on with Naive RAG using no-code tools. Session 3 (Framing & Managing AI Projects): use the taxonomy as a decision framework for AI project scoping — when to use which paradigm, cost/complexity trade-offs. Session 4 (Business Models & Strategy): RAG-as-a-Service business models, build vs buy economics at each paradigm level.

confidence.caveats: The taxonomy is a simplification — real-world RAG systems often blend elements of multiple paradigms. The boundary between Advanced RAG and Modular RAG is fuzzy and debated. Some researchers argue that the taxonomy is becoming outdated as 'Agentic RAG' and 'Context Engineering' emerge as new paradigms (2025-2026). Performance comparisons between paradigms are qualitative — no single controlled benchmark directly compares all three under identical conditions. Market adoption percentages are estimated from industry surveys and may not reflect the global distribution. Cost estimates vary significantly by use case, scale, and vendor pricing changes. The Gao et al. taxonomy was formalized by Chinese university researchers and is most heavily cited in the Chinese and English-language AI research communities.
confidence.security_posture: Security risks escalate with paradigm complexity. Naive RAG: knowledge base poisoning (injecting malicious documents into vector store, shown effective with just 5 documents in millions — PoisonedRAG, USENIX Security 2025), basic prompt injection via retrieved context, embedding inversion attacks (reconstructing original text from vectors). Advanced RAG: all Naive risks plus reranker manipulation (adversarial documents optimized to rank highly), query expansion exploitation (injected content surfaced through expanded queries). Modular RAG: largest attack surface — routing module manipulation (directing queries to compromised modules), fusion module poisoning (conflicting information from multiple sources), agentic module prompt injection chains. Mitigations: embedding-aware filtering (activation distribution analysis), retrieval context separation from system prompts, PromptGuard (Meta) for injection detection, data source trust verification, regular red-teaming. References: arXiv:2509.20324 (RAG threat model formalization), AWS RAG pipeline security guide, Lasso Security RAG analysis. OWASP includes RAG-specific guidance in their LLM Top 10.
